picks.rationale: This is the biggest swing on the board if her HRD score comes back positive: in the HRD-positive subgroup of PAOLA-1 the PFS hazard ratio was 0.33 and 5-year OS hit 66% vs 48%, with median PFS 37.2 vs 17.7 months. She is already on bevacizumab, so this adds olaparib rather than starting a new regimen, which is the cleanest path to that effect size. I will not pretend the gating away: the whole bet rides on the pending genomic-instability call, and stacking a PARP inhibitor on bevacizumab pushes her bleeding and VTE risk given the prior IVC filter. If HRD is positive I want her on this and would tolerate close hematologic and blood-pressure monitoring to get there.
primary_concerns: Entire benefit is gated on the unresulted HRD/somatic-BRCA score; HRD-negative collapses the olaparib add-on to roughly the bevacizumab-alone curve
Grade 3+ anemia 17% and hypertension 19% on top of bevacizumab compound her VTE/bleeding caution and brush her myelosuppression veto

picks.rationale: This is the pick that does not wait for the assay. PRIMA showed a PFS benefit across all-comers (HR 0.62) that deepens to HR 0.43 if she turns out HRD-positive, so the floor is real even on a pending score, and the niraparib preclinical work shows roughly 3.3x tumor-to-plasma exposure that drives activity in BRCA-wild-type models. The honest cost is marrow: grade 3+ thrombocytopenia ran 28.7% in the primary analysis, which lands squarely on her stated myelosuppression veto. The individualized weight- and platelet-based starting dose pulls those rates down, and I would lean on it hard rather than walk away from an active oral drug she could start now.
primary_concerns: Thrombocytopenia and anemia engage her explicit severe-myelosuppression/febrile-neutropenia veto; needs individualized dosing and tight CBC monitoring to stay tolerable
All-comer benefit is modest (HR 0.62); the large effect still depends on her landing HRD-positive

picks.intervention_label: GEN-1 (IMNN-001) program, incl. OVATION-3 maintenance trial
picks.rationale: She is already on this IL-12 immunogene axis and she wants a trial, so the upside play is to keep the bet alive through the OVATION-3 phase 3 (NCT06915025), which lets her layer PARP maintenance on top of IMNN-001. The topline OVATION-2 signal is striking for an early readout: median OS 40.5 vs 29.4 months (HR 0.74), and the BRCAm/HRD subgroup OS HR was 0.42. The evidence is thin and I will say so plainly: no peer-reviewed primary paper, no PMID, a wide confidence interval on 34 patients (0.11-1.70), and no structured safety table in the public material. For a trial-preferring patient already responding on this regimen, the chance to combine IL-12 with PARP in one protocol is worth chasing.
primary_concerns: Efficacy rests on conference topline only (SITC 2024 / ASCO 2025), no peer-reviewed primary publication or PMID, and the BRCAm/HRD subgroup CI spans 0.11-1.70 on n=34
Intraperitoneal weekly dosing is higher-burden than her oral preference, and the full per-term toxicity profile is not public

picks.rationale: If the tumor NGS returns a somatic BRCA1/2 mutation, single-agent olaparib is the highest-effect option in the whole dossier: SOLO1 gave a PFS HR of 0.30, median PFS 56.0 vs 13.8 months, and a 7-year OS HR of 0.55. The mechanistic floor is solid, with the Bryant synthetic-lethality work and a BRCA2-mutant ovarian PDX both showing the response tracks the HR defect. It sits at rank 4 only because eligibility is strictly somatic-BRCA-gated and her germline is wild-type, so this is the reserve play that activates the moment the variant call comes back positive. Long-term myeloid risk (AML reported in 1.2%) is the real-world tail I would watch against her marrow veto.
primary_concerns: Strictly gated on a somatic BRCA1/2 mutation she may not carry; with wild-type germline this could be a dead end
Grade 3+ anemia 22% plus a 1.2% fatal-AML signal over long follow-up press against her severe-myelosuppression veto

notes: Risktaker read: the deep platinum response, R0 resection, and ctDNA cleared to Not Detected all point toward HR-deficient biology, so I am willing to pre-commit to the high-effect HRD-gated plays (PAOLA-1 olaparib+bev, then SOLO1 olaparib if somatic BRCA is mutated) rather than default to the safe low-magnitude options. Niraparib is my hedge because it does not wait on the assay. I deliberately did not rank letrozole or anastrozole: the endocrine signal is real but small (letrozole 60% vs 38.5% recurrence-free at 24 months in a tier-4 cohort, anastrozole is cross-tumor only in granulosa-cell disease), and a low-magnitude holding option is not where a risktaker spends a rank-1 slot for a newly-diagnosed, deeply-responding patient with curative-intent maintenance on the table. Every confidence is low and honestly so, because the single highest-value input (the HRD/somatic-BRCA result) is still pending.

picks.rationale: Continuing the bevacizumab maintenance she already tolerates is the lowest-regret choice while the HRD and somatic-BRCA assay is still out. GOG-218 and ICON7 give this regimen more than a decade of post-approval safety data in her exact 1L indication, with hypertension (G>=2 about 22.9% in GOG-218) as the dominant and well-managed toxicity and no marrow or neuropathic signal that touches her stated vetoes. The PFS gain is modest (HR 0.717, no ITT OS benefit), and her VTE history plus prior IVC filter keep bleeding and thrombosis on the monitoring list, but that risk is already accepted in her current plan.
primary_concerns: Bleeding and thrombotic risk on an anti-VEGF agent given her high-VTE history and prior IVC filter, though this risk is already part of her current regimen
Modest PFS benefit with no ITT overall-survival gain on final analysis; the survival signal in ICON7 was confined to the high-risk subgroup

picks.rationale: Niraparib is the one PARP option with a PRIMA benefit across the all-comers ITT (HR 0.62), so it does not strictly wait on the pending HRD score the way SOLO1 and PAOLA-1 do. I rank it second rather than first because its G>=3 anemia (31%) and thrombocytopenia (28.7%) on the fixed starting dose sit squarely against her myelosuppression veto. The individualized starting dose by weight and platelet count is the mitigation that keeps it on the table, and the magnitude sharpens to HR 0.43 if the pending genomic-instability score comes back positive.
primary_concerns: G>=3 anemia 31% and thrombocytopenia 28.7% on the fixed 300 mg start engage her severe-myelosuppression veto; the individualized starting dose is the prerequisite mitigation
Cumulative G>=3 thrombocytopenia rose to 39.7% in the 3.5-year update, so ongoing count monitoring is required across the maintenance window

picks.rationale: For a 70-79-year-old who wants oral, low-burden therapy, letrozole fits her ER-positive high-grade serous biology with none of the marrow or neuropathic toxicity her vetoes name; the class effects are hot flushes, arthralgia, and fatigue with established management. I keep it at rank 3 because the supporting evidence is a single non-randomized cohort (tier 4, ROBINS-I serious, 60% vs 38.5% recurrence-free at 24 months, p=0.035), not the RCT base behind bevacizumab and the PARP options. Her PR-negativity also tempers the expected endocrine magnitude, so I read this as a low-toxicity holding option rather than a primary maintenance backbone.
primary_concerns: Evidence base is a single non-randomized cohort (tier 4, ROBINS-I serious); no RCT-grade support for maintenance efficacy
PR-negativity and the weak-to-moderate ER intensity temper the expected magnitude of endocrine benefit

notes: Rank order is deliberately gated on the pending tumor HRD and somatic-BRCA result. If that assay returns HRD-positive or shows a somatic BRCA mutation, my view shifts toward an HRD-gated PARP strategy (olaparib + bevacizumab per PAOLA-1, or olaparib per SOLO1 if somatic BRCA-mutated), though I would still weigh the added bleeding/VTE load of stacking a PARP inhibitor onto ongoing bevacizumab against her IVC-filter history. Until the score returns, the safest defensible position is to continue the already-tolerated bevacizumab and hold the PARP decision. I am flagging niraparib's myelosuppression profile and any PARP-plus-bevacizumab stack as candidates for a round-2 toxicity dissent or veto if another persona ranks them first without naming the dose mitigation or the bleeding caution.

picks.rationale: PRIMA is a low-RoB double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 (n=733) with a registered PFS primary endpoint that was hit in the all-comers ITT, HR 0.62 (0.50-0.76), p<0.001. The reason I rank it first is narrow: the benefit holds without the pending HRD score, so the conclusion does not hang on an assay that has not come back. The larger HRD-positive estimate, HR 0.43 (0.31-0.59), is a pre-specified subgroup, not post-hoc fishing.
primary_concerns: Grade 3+ cytopenias dominate the safety profile (anemia 31%, thrombocytopenia 28.7%) and engage her myelosuppression veto; the individualized starting dose lowers but does not erase that risk.
Open question on durable OS: PRIMA reported a PFS benefit; mature ITT overall-survival data are weaker than the SOLO1 OS readout.

picks.rationale: SOLO1 has the lowest RoB and the largest effect in the set, PFS HR 0.30 (0.23-0.41), and it now carries a mature 7-year OS benefit, HR 0.55 (0.40-0.76), p=0.0004. That kind of replicated long-term survival readout is exactly what I want from a maintenance drug. I cannot rank it first because eligibility is conditional: SOLO1 enrolled only BRCA-mutated tumors, her germline is wild-type, and somatic BRCA is still pending, so the pick rests on an unresulted gate.
primary_concerns: Eligibility is gated by the pending tumor NGS; on a germline-wild-type tumor with no somatic BRCA call yet, indication match is unconfirmed.
Grade 3+ anemia (22%) and a 1.2% fatal-AML signal over long follow-up sit against her marrow-toxicity veto.

picks.rationale: PAOLA-1 is the closest design match because every patient was on bevacizumab, which she already receives, and the ITT PFS was positive, HR 0.59 (0.49-0.72). My caution is that the effect concentrates in the HRD-positive subgroup (HR 0.33) and the ITT OS was not significant, so the headline OS gain (66% vs 48% at 5 years) comes from a pre-specified subgroup rather than a confirmed ITT result. The olaparib add-on only pays off if the pending HRD score is positive, and it stacks bleeding risk onto ongoing bevacizumab given her VTE history and prior IVC filter.
primary_concerns: HRD-gated benefit: without the pending genomic-instability score, the add-on value over bevacizumab alone is unestablished for her.
Subgroup-driven OS claim; the ITT OS was not significant, so the survival argument leans on a non-confirmatory subgroup.
Compounded bleeding/VTE risk on top of bevacizumab.

picks.rationale: The anti-angiogenic axis she is already on is the one maintenance option here that is replicated across two phase-3 RCTs, GOG-218 (RoB2:Low) and ICON7 (RoB2:Some, open-label). I keep it lower because both are PFS-only with no ITT OS benefit, and the PFS effect is modest, HR 0.717 (0.625-0.824). ICON7's survival gain was confined to the high-risk subgroup, which is a subgroup result, not an ITT win.
primary_concerns: No ITT OS benefit in either trial; the value is PFS-only.
ICON7 is open-label (RoB2:Some), so its outcome ascertainment is less protected than the double-blind PARP trials.
Bleeding/thrombosis caution given her VTE history, though that risk is already accepted on her current regimen.

notes: I am not abstaining: the dossier holds four low-RoB phase-3 RCTs in her exact 1L-maintenance setting, which clears my bar. The endocrine and immunogene options do not. Letrozole rests on a non-randomized cohort (ROBINS-I:Serious, n=80) and anastrozole on a single-arm phase 2 in granulosa-cell tumors, not her serous histology, with a DCR surrogate rather than PFS or OS. GEN-1 (IMNN-001) is a randomized phase I/II with no peer-reviewed primary paper or PMID yet and only topline numbers, so I can describe its design but not its bias profile, and I will not rank an unpublished result above replicated RCT evidence. The single highest-value action remains the pending HRD/somatic-BRCA assay, which decides whether the olaparib-based options move above niraparib.

picks.rationale: Of the PARP options, niraparib is the one I can recommend today without waiting on her tumor HRD result. NCCN Ovarian v3.2025 lists it as a category 2A first-line maintenance option for all-comers in stage III-IV after a platinum response, and PRIMA carries it (ITT HR_PFS 0.62), with a larger effect if she turns out HRD-positive (HR 0.43). She fits the enrolled population: stage IIIc, R0, deep platinum and ctDNA response. The honest caveat is her myelosuppression veto, since thrombocytopenia and anemia are the dominant grade 3+ events; the weight-and-platelet individualized starting dose is how the guideline-aligned regimen manages that.
primary_concerns: Grade 3+ thrombocytopenia and anemia bump directly against her stated myelosuppression / febrile-neutropenia veto; mitigated but not erased by the individualized starting dose.
PRIMA enrolled ECOG 0-1, which she meets, but her age band (70-79) sits at the older end of the trial population.
Benefit magnitude still firms up once the pending genomic-instability score returns.

picks.rationale: If the pending HRD score comes back positive, this becomes my rank-1 pick rather than a contingent one. PAOLA-1 is the closest design match because every patient was on bevacizumab, which she already receives, and NCCN Ovarian v3.2025 gives olaparib plus bevacizumab a category 1 recommendation for HRD-positive disease (ESMO concurs). The HRD-positive subgroup effect is the strongest on the table (HR_PFS 0.33; 5-year OS 66% vs 48%). I rank it second only because the olaparib add-on is HRD-gated and that result is not back; recommending it now would be getting ahead of the guideline's own biomarker condition.
primary_concerns: Strictly HRD-gated: NCCN reserves the category 1 endorsement for HRD-positive tumors, so the recommendation is conditional on the pending assay.
Stacking a PARP inhibitor on ongoing bevacizumab compounds her bleeding/VTE caution (history of high VTE risk, prior IVC filter); added grade 3+ hypertension 19% and anemia 17%.
If HRD turns out negative, the olaparib add-on loses its guideline footing and the choice collapses back toward bevacizumab alone.

picks.rationale: She is already on this, and continuing it is the lowest-friction guideline-aligned move. NCCN Ovarian v3.2025 keeps bevacizumab maintenance as a category 2A option in her exact 1L indication, with GOG-218 and ICON7 as the evidence base (PFS HR 0.72 and 0.81), and ICON7 showed its largest gain in the high-risk subgroup she matched before R0 resection. It is also the natural backbone if HRD comes back positive and olaparib is layered on per PAOLA-1. The known limit is that the survival benefit was confined to high-risk patients and no ITT OS gain emerged on final analysis.
primary_concerns: PFS-only benefit in the ITT; OS gain limited to the high-risk subgroup.
Bleeding and thrombotic risk on an anti-VEGF agent given her VTE history and prior IVC filter, though that risk is already accepted in her current plan.

picks.rationale: This is the highest-quality evidence in the set, but the guideline gate does not currently open for her. SOLO1 restricts olaparib monotherapy maintenance to BRCA-mutated tumors, and NCCN Ovarian v3.2025 carries the category 1 recommendation only for that population; her germline BRCA is wild-type and somatic BRCA is pending. If the tumor NGS returns a somatic BRCA1/2 mutation, the SOLO1 numbers are remarkable (PFS HR 0.30, mPFS 56 vs 13.8 months, OS HR 0.55). Until then it sits below niraparib and the bevacizumab-anchored options precisely because its guideline endorsement is conditional on a result she does not yet have.
primary_concerns: Requires a somatic BRCA1/2 mutation; germline is wild-type and the somatic call is pending, so she is currently outside the SOLO1 / NCCN category 1 population.
Long-term myeloid risk (AML in 1.2% of SOLO1) is relevant to her marrow-toxicity caution.

picks.rationale: I include this as the low-toxicity option that fits her age and her preference for oral, low-burden therapy, but I rank it last because the guideline support is thin. NCCN Ovarian v3.2025 lists aromatase inhibitors among hormone-therapy options for ER-positive disease, yet the direct maintenance evidence here is a non-randomized cohort (60% vs 38.5% recurrence-free at 24 months), well below the PARP and bevacizumab RCTs. Her ER-positive biology and PR-negativity make this a reasonable holding strategy or later-line choice rather than the frontline maintenance the guidelines anchor on.
primary_concerns: Evidence tier is a non-randomized cohort, far below the category 1/2A PARP and bevacizumab data that drive frontline maintenance.
PR-negativity tempers the expected magnitude of endocrine benefit.

notes: Guideline-fit ranking for a newly-diagnosed, platinum-responsive, R0 stage IIIc HGSC, germline BRCA wild-type, HRD pending. The pending tumor HRD / somatic-BRCA assay is the real fork in the road, and I have ranked around it rather than guessing at it. Niraparib leads because it is the one PARP NCCN v3.2025 endorses for all-comers without that result. Olaparib + bevacizumab is the conditional front-runner if HRD reads positive, and olaparib monotherapy if somatic BRCA reads positive; I have kept both below niraparib to respect the biomarker conditions the guidelines themselves attach. Bevacizumab continuation is the safe guideline-aligned default in the interim. I did not consider the on-study GEN-1/IMNN-001 program as a competing pick: it is investigational and outside any consensus guideline, so it stays in the on-study context rather than my recommendation list.

picks.rationale: She is already on bevacizumab, and continuing it asks nothing new of her: no marrow suppression and no neuropathy, so neither of her two vetoes is touched. The IV q3w schedule is the one infusion burden she has already accepted, and the bleeding/VTE caution from her high-risk history and prior IVC filter is a risk already built into her current plan rather than a new one. GOG-218 and ICON7 back this axis in her exact 1L setting, with the largest ICON7 survival gain in the high-risk subgroup she matched before her R0 resection.
primary_concerns: Fully satisfies both toxicity vetoes (no myelosuppression, no neuropathy)
In tension with the thrombotic/bleeding modality caution, though that risk is already accepted on her current regimen
Partial tension with oral/low-infusion preference: IV q3w, but the burden she is already carrying
Holds the maintenance axis steady while the rank-1 HRD/somatic-BRCA assay returns and decides whether a PARP add-on belongs on top

picks.rationale: Of every option on the table, this is the one that clears her whole preference set without a single conflict: oral once daily, no myelosuppression, no neuropathy, and none of the bleeding or thrombotic risk that follows her around. It targets her own ER-positive high-grade serous biology, which fits her age band and her stated preference for low-burden oral therapy. I am ranking it second rather than first only because the evidence is a non-randomized cohort and her PR-negativity tempers how much endocrine benefit to expect, not because it fails her preferences. It is the natural low-toxicity maintenance or holding option if she wants to stay off cytopenia-prone drugs.
primary_concerns: Clears every preference axis: oral, no marrow toxicity, no neuropathy, no bleeding/VTE risk
Weakest evidence tier of the picks (tier 4 cohort, ROBINS-I serious)
PR-negativity tempers the expected magnitude of endocrine benefit

picks.rationale: This is the PARP option I can put forward without waiting on the pending HRD score, since PRIMA showed a benefit across all-comers, and it is oral once daily, which fits her modality preference. The catch is real: grade 3+ anemia near 31% and thrombocytopenia near 29% bump directly against her severe-myelosuppression veto. The individualized starting dose lowers those rates and is the only way I would bring this forward for her, and even then the magnitude she gets still sharpens once the genomic-instability score returns. I rank it below bevacizumab and letrozole because that cytopenia profile is exactly the toxicity she asked to avoid.
primary_concerns: Direct tension with the severe-myelosuppression veto (grade 3+ anemia ~31%, thrombocytopenia ~29%); individualized dosing mitigates but does not erase it
Satisfies the oral modality preference
Does not strictly gate on the pending HRD result, though benefit is larger if HRD-positive

picks.rationale: She told us she prefers trials, and she is already enrolled on the GEN-1/IMNN-001 program, so honoring that preference partly means keeping the on-study path open. The randomized OVATION 2 signal (median OS 40.5 vs 29.4 months) is encouraging, and the registrational OVATION 3 protocol explicitly allows olaparib or niraparib maintenance alongside IMNN-001, which links her IL-12 axis to the same PARP question her pending HRD result will settle. Intraperitoneal IL-12 has read as manageable in prior GEN-1 work, with no marrow or neuropathy signal that trips her vetoes. I keep it on the list as the trial-continuity option rather than ranking it higher because it is investigational and its PARP arm only applies to her if the HRD/somatic-BRCA call comes back the right way.
primary_concerns: Honors the stated prefers_trials preference and her existing on-study enrollment
No reported marrow or neuropathy toxicity that engages her vetoes
Investigational; the PARP-maintenance arm is itself gated on the pending HRD/somatic-BRCA result

notes: The patient's own framing makes the tumor HRD / somatic-BRCA assay the rank-1 shared move, and I agree with it, but it lives in target_validation rather than the intervention evidence files, so I cannot list it as an intervention_id here. I am flagging it as the gate that sits above all four picks: it decides whether an HRD-gated PARP regimen (olaparib or olaparib + bevacizumab per PAOLA-1) belongs on top of her existing bevacizumab, and it refines how much niraparib would buy her. I deliberately left olaparib and olaparib + bevacizumab off the ranked list for now because their benefit only pays off if the pending score is positive and the olaparib-plus-bevacizumab combination would stack a second anemia source onto her bleeding/VTE caution. Read straight from her preferences: bevacizumab and letrozole clear both toxicity vetoes outright; niraparib is the one pick in open tension with the severe-myelosuppression veto, surfaced rather than hidden because it is the only PARP that does not wait on the pending assay.
